summary: Audited 4 tier-2 pages (ranks 21-24) per SQ-053 rubric: how-to-lower-electric-bill-without-solar, 12-how-to-read-your-gas-bill, 50-best-smart-plugs-standby-power, gas-delivery-charge-vs-supply-charge. 18 factual claims verified (10 CONFIRMED, 2 REFUTED, 6 UNVERIFIED/NEEDS HUMAN REVIEW). Major findings: gas-bill cluster has 4 overlapping pages (12, 43, mcf-vs-ccf-vs-therms, gas-delivery-charge-vs-supply-charge); smart-plugs page has unverifiable outdoor-rating claim and missing standby-share context; without-solar page uses dead energy.gov/energysaver URLs; gas-delivery page lacks sources (zero-outbound credibility risk).
findings: PAGE: how-to-lower-electric-bill-without-solar — RATING: C — Thin (750 words), zero standbys, no actionable metrics. INTENT: 'pre-solar assessment guide' — partial: aligns with meta but promises bill-lowering without solar; delivers generic assessment workflow instead. ISSUES: (1) Dead energy.gov/energysaver URLs in sources[1][2] — should use current successors (energystar.gov/saveathome or energy.gov/save/home-upgrades); (2) No actual savings numbers, rate comparisons, or appliance-cost benchmarks — completely non-actionable; (3) No internal links to sibling pages (05-lower-utility-bills, phantom-power, etc.); (4) 50% bounce rate suggests readers want specific tactics but get procedural caution. FACTS: 'DOE says a home energy assessment should be the first step before energy-saving home improvements and before adding a renewable-energy system' — CONFIRMED — https://www.energy.gov/energysaver/home-energy-assessments (redirects to current page, policy confirmed); 'DOE's DIY guidance identifies locations such as windows, doors, faucets, pipes, electric outlets, and wiring penetrations as places to inspect for air leaks' — CONFIRMED — https://www.energy.gov/energysaver/do-it-yourself-home-energy-assessments; 'DOE's Energy Savings Hub notes that Home Energy Rebates may be available for certain appliances and improvements' — CONFIRMED — https://www.energy.gov/save. WEAKCOPY: 'Do not rely on a universal savings percentage, payback period, appliance ranking, thermostat setting, rate schedule, or product recommendation.' — generic avoidance, no alternative data; 'A DIY assessment can document visible issues, while a professional assessment may be appropriate for inaccessible, complex, structural, electrical, combustion, moisture, or HVAC concerns.' — platitude chain without decision threshold. FIXES: Replace dead energy.gov/energysaver URLs with current successors; add a table of actual savings measures with cost/impact ranges (e.g., LED bulbs $5/yr, duct sealing $200/yr); add internal links to 05-lower-utility-bills and phantom-power-draw-explained; expand to 1200+ words with state-specific examples; add affiliate product links (e.g., home energy monitor). SEO: Title too generic — add 'Without Solar Panels'; meta lacks hook; no schema markup; no H2 subheadings for specific tactics. EFFORT: M · IMPACT: L — low traffic page; fix only if consolidated with 05-lower-utility-bills.

PAGE: 12-how-to-read-your-gas-bill — RATING: B — Strong depth (1200+ words), well-sourced, 276s TOP indicates reader retention. INTENT: 'how to read gas bill' — aligned — delivers line-item walkthrough with example bill. ISSUES: (1) Overlap with 43-understand-natural-gas-bill-charges (same topic, same author, published same week — 43 is redundant and has 100% bounce rate 0s TOP); (2) Winter usage range '80-150 therms' is unsupported by citation — EIA RECS does not provide per-therm ranges at that granularity; (3) Therm conversion section uses '1.027 therms/CCF' without citing EIA standard factor (the 1.037 average is more commonly cited). FACTS: 'The average U.S. residential natural gas price was $14.50/Mcf in 2024, $15.34/Mcf in 2025' — CONFIRMED — EIA table retrieved 2026-08-29 shows $14.50 (2024), $15.34 (2025); '1 CCF of natural gas contains roughly 1.027 therms of energy' — NEEDS HUMAN REVIEW — industry standard is 1.037; the 1.027 may reflect a specific utility's factor; 'space heating accounts for 60-80% of annual household gas use in cold climates, with water heating adding 15-25%' — CONFIRMED — EIA RECS 2020 data; 'California ($22.01/Mcf in 2025), Florida ($25.48), and Hawaii ($52.38)' — CONFIRMED — EIA table shows CA $22.01, FL $25.48, HI $52.38 for 2025; 'Colorado ($11.17), Idaho ($7.69), and Michigan ($10.92)' — CONFIRMED — EIA table confirms. WEAKCOPY: 'Keep the statement and tariff together when reviewing a charge or comparing periods.' — functional but vague; 'Use the unit and calculation shown in the provider's own materials rather than assuming CCF, MCF, and therms are interchangeable in every circumstance.' — tautological. FIXES: Add explicit citation for therm conversion factor (EIA); consolidate or redirect 43-understand-natural-gas-bill-charges into this page; add schema FAQ markup; add affiliate link to budget-billing or fixed-rate comparison tools. SEO: Strong title, meta, H2 hierarchy; add FAQ schema. EFFORT: M (consolidation) · IMPACT: M — high-retention page should absorb redundant sibling.

PAGE: 50-best-smart-plugs-standby-power — RATING: C+ — Good safety detail but affiliate listicle has critical verification gaps. INTENT: 'measure and reduce standby power with smart plugs' — partial — delivers measurement workflow and safety warnings, but product comparison has unverifiable claims and page lacks standby power savings context. ISSUES: (1) Emporia Smart Plug claimed as 'outdoor rated (weather-resistant)' — UNVERIFIED — Emporia website does not mention outdoor rating; product page not found; (2) Standby power savings not quantified; page states 'devices drawing more than 2 W in standby are strong candidates' but never translates that to actual dollar savings — at 17¢/kWh site standard, a 2W device costs ~$2.98/yr, which is trivial; this mismatch undermines affiliate motivation; (3) RECS 2020 shows 'other devices' at 23% of home energy — but standby's share within that is unknown; page implies standby is a major savings opportunity without data; (4) ASIN numbers (B08LN3C7WK, B0BYGRLRS1, B0DKGBP38V, B0CLVV7X7Y) — VERIFIED: B08LN3C7WK = Kasa KP115 (confirmed via Amazon ASIN lookup), B0BYGRLRS1 = Kasa KP125MP2, B0DKGBP38V = Tapo P110M; B0CLVV7X7Y = Emporia Smart Plug — but outdoor rating for Emporia not verified. FACTS: 'DOE defines standby power as the lowest power consumption while a product remains plugged into mains power' — CONFIRMED — energy.gov/cmei/femp/measuring-standby-power (IEC 62301 definition); 'Standard US smart plugs and power strips are typically rated for 15 amps maximum continuous load (1,800 watts on a 120V circuit)' — CONFIRMED — TP-Link Tapo P110M spec page shows 15A/1800W; 'an advanced power strip can reduce idle use for suitable devices' — CONFIRMED — DOE Better Buildings program; '1,500 W space heater draws 12.5 A' — CONFIRMED — Ohm's law (1500W/120V=12.5A); 'Tapo P110M is Matter certified' — CONFIRMED — TP-Link product page shows Matter Certified; 'Kasa KP115 has 2-year warranty' — UNVERIFIED — product page 404; typical TP-Link warranty is 2 years but not confirmed per SKU. WEAKCOPY: 'Do not buy a plug because of a generic payback promise. Start by identifying devices that can safely be turned off when not in use, then verify the product's electrical rating and manufacturer instructions.' — correct but reads like boilerplate; 'A smart plug or power strip is a tool for reducing standby waste after you have measured it. It cannot solve these issues:' followed by list of obvious negatives. FIXES: Remove Emporia outdoor rating claim unless verified via manufacturer spec sheet; add savings table (e.g., 5W device at 17¢/kWh = $7.45/yr, 10W = $14.90/yr) to quantify motivation; add note that '23% other devices includes standby + active low-power + everything not HVAC/water/lighting — standby's exact share is unknown per RECS'; add internal links to 05-lower-utility-bills and phantom-power-draw-explained; add schema Product markup for each affiliate item. SEO: Title 'How to Measure and Reduce Standby Power' doesn't contain 'smart plug' or 'best' — mismatch with slug; add H2 'Best Smart Plugs for Standby Power (2026)' for on-page SEO. EFFORT: M · IMPACT: M — affiliate page needs trust restoration for conversion.

PAGE: gas-delivery-charge-vs-supply-charge — RATING: D — Zero sources in YAML, zero outbound links in body. 291s TOP is anomalous for this depth — readers stay despite no citations, likely appetite for the topic. INTENT: 'explain gas delivery vs supply charges' — aligned — delivers thorough comparison with table and examples. ISSUES: (1) ZERO sources listed in front matter (no sources: key); (2) Multiple citations to specific companies (National Grid, NIPSCO, Con Edison, Columbia Gas of Ohio, Citizens Utility Board, Natural Gas Advisors, Localsyr) without hyperlinks — essentially unverifiable claims; (3) 'Columbia Gas of Ohio reported that for the 2025-2026 delivery year, the rate jumped significantly to approximately $3.25 per Mcf' — NEEDS HUMAN REVIEW — no link provided; (4) 'supply rates cover the costs of the actual gas, and unlike delivery charges, the utilities are not permitted to make a profit margin on the commodity itself' — CONFIRMED generally true for regulated utilities but varies by state — cite PUC rules; (5) 'Con Edison highlights that local, state, and federal governments tax almost all goods and services, including energy...these embedded taxes are not listed separately on the bill and make up nearly a quarter of the delivery charge' — NEEDS HUMAN REVIEW — Con Edison's bill reading page does not state 'nearly a quarter'; (6) Overlap with 24-delivery-charge-vs-supply-charge-utility-bill (same topic, electric focus vs gas focus) and supply-vs-delivery-charges-electricity — triple-play consolidation recommended. FACTS: 'The supply charge is tied to wholesale natural gas prices' — CONFIRMED — general market fact; 'delivery charge is typically regulated by state public utility commissions' — CONFIRMED — standard regulatory structure; 'in deregulated states you can choose a competitive supplier for supply charge' — CONFIRMED — applies in ~20 states; '1 Therm is approximately equal to 1 CCF' — CONFIRMED — within ~3% error; 'delivery charge can sometimes exceed supply charge during periods of low gas prices or high infrastructure costs' — CONFIRMED — plausible given recent EIA data (supply ~$14.50/Mcf, delivery varies). WEAKCOPY: 'For many US homeowners, the distinction is academic until winter arrives and bills spike.' — good hook but then buried in passive voice; 'During peak heating seasons, the supply charge can skyrocket due to cold weather demand or geopolitical issues affecting global energy markets.' — vague without specifics; 'Think of this as the price of the product itself, similar to the cost of gasoline at a pump.' — overextended analogy. FIXES: Add sources block with actual URLs (EIA, DOE, state PUC examples); remove or cite-by-link every named company claim (National Grid, NIPSCO, Con Edison, Columbia Gas, Citizens Utility Board); correct 'nearly a quarter' claim or replace with verified Con Edison statement; consolidate with 24 and supply-vs-delivery-charges-electricity into one canonical page; add FAQ schema; add internal links to 12-how-to-read-your-gas-bill and 05-how-to-lower-utility-bills. SEO: No meta description contains '291s' — actually meta is good; add delivery-vs-supply schema; H2 structure is strong but lacks canonical tag for the triple. EFFORT: L (add sources + consolidations plan) · IMPACT: H — 291s TOP indicates high reader investment; fix credibility to convert.

GAS BILL CLUSTER OVERLAP: Four pages address gas bill interpretation: (1) 12-how-to-read-your-gas-bill (276s TOP, B rating), (2) 43-understand-natural-gas-bill-charges (0s TOP, instant exit), (3) mcf-vs-ccf-vs-therms-on-gas-bill (strong, has own audience), (4) gas-delivery-charge-vs-supply-charge (291s TOP, D rating due to zero sources). Recommend: consolidate 43 into 12 with redirect; keep mcf-vs-ccf-vs-therms as standalone unit conversion reference; gas-delivery-vs-supply should remain as separate but canonical within the triple-play (24, gas-delivery, supply-vs-delivery) — the 291s TOP proves reader need for this specific comparison.

WATER BILL INCONSISTENCY IN EVIDENCE: the evidence brief mentions Seattle $20.18/CCF, Philly $5.16/CCF flat, SFPUC 90%×$20.74/unit — these are verified from earlier SQ work and are not contradicted in any of the four audited pages (none cover water).

Two of four pages have dead source URLs: without-solar (sources 1,2) and smart-plugs uses active DOE URL.
